name: Sodium/potassium manipulation (peak week)

lead: Peak week is the final stretch of bodybuilding contest preparation, in which competitors adjust sodium, potassium, carbohydrate and water intake to look drier and more defined on stage. Some appearance-focused people borrow the idea for photo shoots.

The chain: changing electrolytes and fluids is said to shift how much water sits under the skin and in muscle, while carbohydrate loading in the final stage refills glycogen, which holds water, to make muscles look full. Reference sources describe the general approach only briefly, and no controlled study of the sodium and potassium part was found.

paras: It is done in the last days before the event, as the final phase of a long cut, with carbohydrate, salt and fluid intake changed on a planned schedule. People use it for a specific date, not as an everyday routine, and the visible change is expected on the day itself.

Intentional dehydration is among the practices linked in reference material to higher death rates among bodybuilders. Dehydration of even a few percent of body water can impair thinking and cause dizziness, and larger losses are dangerous. Electrolyte shifts carry their own health risks.

web.title: Peak week recommendations for bodybuilders: an evidence based approach

chain: Shifts in water under the skin
Drier, more defined look on the day
angle.text: Bodybuilders adjust sodium, potassium and fluids in the final days before a show or shoot to look drier and more defined, by shifting water under the skin. It is a documented part of contest prep, and practitioners report the visual effect; controlled studies of it are limited.

lead: Sodium and potassium manipulation during peak week refers to deliberate changes to salt, potassium and fluid intake in the days before a bodybuilding contest or photo shoot, with the stated aim of a drier, more defined look with visible muscle separation and vascularity. It is one part of the final contest-prep stage, which reference sources describe as combining carbohydrate loading with dehydration [1].

Practitioners describe a typical shape in general terms: water and salt intake are first raised and then restricted, while carbohydrate and potassium are used to fill the muscles with glycogen so they look fuller. A 2021 review of peak-week practices by Escalante and colleagues in BMC Sports Science, Medicine and Rehabilitation reports that surveys and interviews document this, and that some competitors also use diuretics or herbal options [1].

Research on peak week consists of surveys, case reports, small studies and narrative reviews rather than controlled trials of the sodium or potassium protocols themselves. The same review states that current evidence does not indicate these practices are specifically effective or safe, while describing the physiology that makes timing matter [1].
infobox: Final days before a show or shoot
None found of sodium or potassium protocols; case reports and small studies exist [1]

paras: Competitors typically spend 12 to 14 weeks cutting, then in the final stage combine carbohydrate loading with dehydration to sharpen muscle definition and vascularity. Sodium and potassium changes are one set of tactics within that final stage. The review by Escalante and colleagues describes athletes loading and then restricting water and sodium to look dry, sometimes adding prescription diuretics such as furosemide and spironolactone or herbal options such as dandelion tea [1]. Specific protocols are not described here.

Studies of competitors show how common the practices are: in a survey cited in the review, 65.4 percent of respondents used water loading, 32.1 percent used water restriction and 25 percent used both [1].

In a survey of 81 natural bodybuilders (59 men and 22 women), 93.8 percent used some peak-week strategy, most often involving carbohydrate, water or sodium manipulation; sodium restriction was reported by 13.6 percent, sodium loading by 18.5 percent and both by 6.2 percent, with changes usually made three to four days before competition [1]. A separate survey of 382 competitors with 30 interviews found frequent sodium depletion and dehydration, with participants acknowledging risks while calling the practices temporary and necessary [1].

Proponents say fluid distribution can be shifted by changing electrolyte and water intake. Glycogen is stored with water, and carbohydrate loading is documented to cause water retention. The BMC review adds that the body responds to water and sodium changes through antidiuretic hormone, aldosterone and the renin-angiotensin system, which work to restore balance and can blunt the intended loss of water; there is a lag of roughly a day or two before these responses fully take hold, which the authors suggest could be exploited though this is unproven [1]. They also argue that retaining muscle glycogen may favour reducing extracellular rather than intracellular water [1].

Potassium features because glycogen storage depends on potassium availability, so the authors consider adequate potassium important during carbohydrate loading and water cutting [1]. They note that sodium is also needed for glucose transport, so restriction that overlaps with carbohydrate loading may work against the loading [1]. Medical sources describe how the kidneys regulate water and sodium, and note that sodium retention drives swelling in some conditions.

The review adds that sodium-glucose cotransporters limit carbohydrate absorption, which is why the authors say sodium should not be cut at the same time as carbohydrate loading, and that renin-angiotensin-aldosterone activation starts within about 24 hours of sodium restriction with aldosterone rising sharply by about 48 hours [1]. It cites work by Costill and colleagues showing that early dehydration draws mostly on intracellular water, with intracellular and extracellular losses becoming roughly equal later [1].

The evidence for sodium, potassium and water protocols is described as limited. In one small study cited in the BMC review, seven competitors reported that water loading was largely ineffective and inconsistent, and they stopped using it [1]. Evidence for water loading and restriction followed by weight loss comes mainly from combat athletes, not bodybuilders [1].

Evidence on the carbohydrate side is also preliminary. The review describes a quasi-experimental study of 24 amateur bodybuilders in which upper-arm muscle size rose about 3 percent in the carbohydrate-manipulation group and judges rated photos better, though subjects were not drug-tested, and a case study in which ultrasound muscle thickness rose about 5 percent in the upper body and 2 percent in the lower body [1].

In the small study by Mitchell and colleagues, all seven natural male bodybuilders loaded and then cut water, and said the results were largely ineffective; three of the seven also manipulated sodium with inconsistent results, and all three decided not to repeat it [1]. The review describes de Moraes and colleagues' study of 24 amateur men, in which a depletion and loading carbohydrate sequence raised upper-arm muscle size about 3 percent with no change in controls, and judges rated the loaded group's physiques as better, though gastrointestinal symptoms were more common [1]. A case series of six men reported a 4.9 percent biceps thickness increase after a carbohydrate load, but lacked a timely baseline so causality is uncertain [1].

Dehydration causes thirst, headache and fatigue, and a loss of 1 to 2 percent of body water can impair thinking; losses of 5 to 8 percent can cause fatigue and dizziness, and more severe losses can be fatal. Reference material lists intentional dehydration among training practices linked to higher death rates in bodybuilders.

The BMC review reports case studies of severe outcomes after peak-week practices, including hyperkalemia, hypokalemia, hyponatremia, water intoxication, rhabdomyolysis and cardiac changes, and says competitors often downplay these risks [1]. Prescription diuretics are banned in sport by WADA, according to the review [1].

Two case reports in the review illustrate the range of outcomes: a 35-year-old man who combined very high water intake, a diuretic and salt restriction developed hyperkalemia, hyponatremia, water intoxication, rhabdomyolysis and ECG changes and recovered after treatment, and a 26-year-old professional who used a loop diuretic in the final two days lost 5 to 6 kg and developed severe hypokalemia, hyperglycemia, hyperlactatemia and tachycardia, also recovering [1].

Escalante and colleagues conclude that water and sodium manipulation should be carefully planned and practised, ideally together with carbohydrate manipulation, and wrote that leaving these variables alone may be a better option for some competitors; they recommend a practice run two to four weeks before competition [1]. They stress that individual variability is high and that bodybuilder-specific studies are few [1].

Their recommendation, as summarised, is to cut sodium only after carbohydrate loading ends, to maintain adequate potassium throughout loading and dehydration, and to keep sodium constant if no practice run is possible; they state overall that the evidence is preliminary and that mistimed strategies carry real risks [1].

No controlled trials of sodium or potassium manipulation protocols in bodybuilders were found. Related human research consists of surveys, case reports and small studies of peak-week carbohydrate, water and nutrition practices, summarised in a 2021 review [1], and wider nutrition research on sodium intake and blood pressure, such as the DASH-Sodium randomized trial of 412 participants, which is not specific to physique contests [2].
